note: Vol. I No. 42. THE BRIDGE OVER THE NORTH BRANCH IS PUT ON RECORD BY A CORONER'S JURY — Elizabeth Fitzpatrick 'residing above the bridge over the North Branch of the Chicago river in this town' — which is a second, different bridge from the draw-bridge of the week before, and a documented dwelling upstream of it. Also here: a store auctioned off P. S. Carli standing on J. S. C. Hogan's lot, the federal advertisement for the weekly horseback mail from Chicago to Green Bay from 1 January 1835, and a silversmith hiring Indian jewelry manufacturers at top wages a month before the annuity payment.

claims.notes: A HOUSE IS PLACED BY A CORONER'S JURY: 'residing above the bridge over the North Branch of the Chicago river in this town'. This is the strongest evidence in the September run for TWO things the reconstruction has to decide. First, THERE WAS A BRIDGE OVER THE NORTH BRANCH in September 1834 and it was the landmark by which that stretch of river was described — distinct from the draw-bridge over the main channel that two South Water Street advertisements use as their anchor (1834-09-10 claim c002, and claim c002 of this issue). Second, the ground ABOVE that bridge — upstream, west and north — was inhabited by people the paper counted as living IN THIS TOWN, which is further out than the militia notice of 3 September implies when it lists 'Chicago' and 'the North Branch' as separate settlements (1834-09-03, claim c006). Nothing is built from this here; it is filed because a placement made by a jury under oath is a better class of evidence than an advertisement's own address, and the project has almost none of it. The passage is one of the alternated leader columns; the completions are read off issue page 2 column 6 and are bracketed because the locator names column 5.

claims.notes: A STOREFRONT SOLD OUT FROM UNDER ITS OCCUPIER, AND PLACED BY WHOSE LOT IT STANDS ON. Two things the reconstruction can use. (1) THE PLACEMENT IS BY LOT OWNERSHIP, not by street: 'the store occupied by P. S. Carli, Esq. as a grocery and fancy store, on J. S. C. Hogan's lot'. Hogan's own store is one door below the Post Office on South Water Street (1834-09-03, claim c013), so his lot is fixed and Carli's building stands on it — a TENANT BUILDING on another man's ground, which is a relation this project's parcel model has no way to express yet. (2) THE BUILDING AND THE STOCK ARE SOLD SEPARATELY and both may be examined beforehand, so the structure was a chattel that changed hands apart from the land. Marked `contradicts` under ruling 3: Carli's occupation of this store is ENDED by this notice, and any later reconstruction that stands a Carli grocery on Hogan's lot in 1835 has to answer it. It does NOT contradict Carli's Eagle Tavern, which is a different concern; the veto attaches to the claim, not to the man.

claims.notes: A DEATH IN THE TOWN WITH A CAUSE AND A JOURNEY: bilious fever and inflammation of the bowels, in a New York merchant of twenty-two returning from Galena, taken sick three weeks before. The SURNAME IS DESTROYED — the column edge leaves only '…ey' — so the person entered here is a name this corpus cannot complete, and it is entered that way rather than guessed at. The route matters as much as the man: Galena to Chicago by land in 1834 is the lead-trade road, and the town was a stop on it.

claims.notes: THE CHICAGO–GREEN BAY MAIL IS A WEEKLY HORSEBACK ROUTE, PUT OUT TO CONTRACT FOR THE THREE YEARS FROM 1 JANUARY 1835 — which is to say, THIS is the mail service the town has at the scene date. One rider a week north. For a reconstruction that has to decide what the post office building was doing and how much traffic its door took, the federal advertisement is a better answer than an inference from the town's size. It also fixes the northern road as a horse route and not a wagon one in 1835.

claims.notes: A CHICAGO SILVERSMITH HIRING TWO OR THREE MEN TO MAKE INDIAN SILVER WORK, AT TOP WAGES, IN SEPTEMBER 1834 — the month before the last great annuity payment at Chicago. The trade goods the treaties were paid in were being MANUFACTURED IN THE TOWN, not just forwarded through it, and Mulford's own standing advertisement lists 'Indian silver work manufactured' among his stock (1834-09-03, issue page 4). This is a workshop, not a counter, and the reconstruction has no craft interiors of this kind recorded anywhere yet.
